A US court found Google’s search business to be a monopoly because it violated Section 2 of the Sherman Act through exclusionary conduct involving default-distribution deals [Source: ev-1]. Specifically, Judge Amit Mehta ruled on August 5, 2024, that Google is a monopolist in general search services and general search text advertising [Source: ev-1]. The theory of harm centered on Google paying companies such as Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla billions of dollars to secure default search engine placement; for instance, trial evidence showed Google paid approximately $26.3 billion for distribution in 2021 and paid Apple roughly 36% of Safari search-ad revenue [Source: ev-1]. This practice created a self-reinforcing loop where defaults generated scale, which produced data, improved quality, and protected the default status against rivals [Source: ev-1].

Regarding remedies, Judge Mehta ordered structural measures on August 5, 2 conduct including requiring Google to sell Chrome (noted as the first forced divestiture of a major tech company since the Microsoft case of 2000) and prohibiting further payments for default search placement or revenue-sharing agreements [Source: ev-1]. Additionally, the ruling imposed limits on acquisitions and AI-related investments [Source: ev-1]. While Google appealed these decisions in 2025, arguing that the trial court punished procompetitive innovation, the final outcome remained pending through 2025 [Source: ev-1].
